summary: This document describes an optional IPv6 destination option that carries sequence numbers and timing information in each packet. The measurements can be examined in real time or later, and help diagnose where delays and performance problems are happening.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like stamping each package with a number and a time, so you can see where in the delivery trip it got slow.

questions: what is the ipv6 pdm destination option
how to measure ipv6 packet delay
how to measure server delay in ipv6
what is the pdm option type
subtitle: An IPv6 destination option that stamps packets with sequence numbers and time deltas, to tell network delay from server delay.

tldr.problem: IPv6 has no field for timing, so it is hard to tell whether slow responses come from the network or from the server.
tldr.mechanism: The Performance and Diagnostic Metrics (PDM) destination option adds a 10-byte option with two packet sequence numbers and two scaled time deltas. No clock synchronization is needed between the hosts.
tldr.outcome: From PDM data one can derive round-trip delay and server delay, so a diagnostician can quickly see whether to look at the network or at the server. It adds security concerns and should be off by default.

today: RFC 8250 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2017, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. IANA registered option type 0x0F for PDM in the Destination Options and Hop-by-Hop Options sub-registry.

sections.title: Background and Rationale
sections.content:
To assess performance problems, sequence numbers and timing can be embedded in each packet and read in real time or after the fact. IPv6 destination options carry information that only the destination node needs to examine, not routers or middleboxes. This RFC defines the Performance and Diagnostic Metrics (PDM) destination option.

The RFC states that IPv6 has no timing field in its main header or any extension header, and lists the advantages of adding one: it measures real transactions, works across organizational boundaries, needs no time synchronization between session partners, and treats all transport protocols (TCP, UDP, SCTP and others) uniformly. It is meant as a fast triage tool for deciding whether a latency problem is in the network or in the server.

A warning applies to transition technologies: a packet with PDM may be dropped, for example by an IPv6-to-IPv4 translator that does not recognize the Destination Options header, or by a device that cannot handle multiple extension headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a packet does not say how long anybody held it. PDM adds a little note with that information so slow spots can be found quickly.

sections.title: Metrics PDM Can Provide
sections.content:
Packets are identified by a 5-tuple: sender address (SADDR), sender port (SPORT), destination address (DADDR), destination port (DPORT) and upper-layer protocol (PROTC). Combined with the 5-tuple, the PDM fields allow two metrics to be measured.

  • Round-trip delay: the time for a packet to go from a source to a destination and back, as defined in RFC 2681.
  • Server delay: the interval between a device receiving a packet and sending the first corresponding packet back. It can include server processing time (the combination of stack and application) and delay caused by acknowledgments.

If a clear split between application time and stack time is needed, the RFC notes that more client-based measurements are required.
sections.plainLanguage: Round trip is how long a question takes to go there and back. Server delay is how long the other side thought about it before answering.

sections.title: The PDM Option Layout
sections.content:
PDM is a type-length-value option carried in the IPv6 Destination Options header (Next Header value 60, defined in RFC 8200). The option type is 0x0F. The two high-order bits MUST be 00 and the third high-order bit MUST be 0, meaning the data cannot change en route. The Option Length MUST be 10.

  • ScaleDTLR and ScaleDTLS: 8-bit scaling values for the two delta fields.
  • PSNTP (Packet Sequence Number This Packet): 16 bits, wraps, starts at a random number and increases for each packet of the 5-tuple flow. The random start makes spoofing harder. Operating systems MUST keep a separate counter per 5-tuple.
  • PSNLR (Last Received): 16 bits, the PSNTP of the packet last received on the 5-tuple, initialized to 0.
  • DELTATLR (Delta Time Last Received): 16 bits, the send time of packet n minus the receive time of packet n-1.
  • DELTATLS (Delta Time Last Sent): 16 bits, the receive time of packet n minus the send time of packet n-1.

The options are aligned so multi-octet values fall on natural boundaries. PDM MUST NOT appear more than once per IPv6 header, though an encapsulated packet MAY carry its own PDM for each encapsulated IPv6 header.
sections.plainLanguage: The note on each packet has four numbers: which packet this is, which one I last saw from you, how long I waited before replying, and how long since I last sent.

sections.title: Time Units and Scaling
sections.content:
The base time unit is 1 attosecond, which gives one common unit for all stacks and hardware. Because a time difference must fit in 16 bits but may range from extremely small to the very large delays of Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking, the value is scaled. The native time value is multiplied by a power of 10 to get attoseconds, then bits are shifted out from the low end until the 16 most significant bits remain. The number of bits dropped is stored as the scale value.

Appendix B works an example: a difference of 39838 microseconds becomes a delta of 8D88 (hex) with a scale of 40. The same appendix says delta values below 65536 attoseconds are stored exactly, and that the maximum loss of precision at a given scale is 2**scale - 1 attoseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Time is written like a number in scientific notation: a short number plus a note saying how many places to shift. That way tiny and huge waits both fit in the same small space.

sections.title: Placement and Implementation Rules
sections.content:
With IPsec ESP there is no 5-tuple because there are no port numbers, so a flow is identified by SADDR, DADDR and PROTC and the Security Parameter Index SHOULD be ignored. In ESP transport mode, PDM MUST be placed after the ESP header so as not to leak information. In tunnel mode, a tunnel endpoint that creates a new packet may use PDM independently of the original packet.

An implementation should provide an interface to enable or disable PDM, and the RFC recommends PDM being off by default. PDM MUST NOT be turned on merely because a packet arrived with a PDM header, since it could be spoofed. When on, it may apply to all packets, one upper-layer protocol, a local port or an IP address. Timestamps SHOULD be taken as close to the physical network interface as possible. Implementations should also configure a maximum lifetime and a maximum memory for stored PDM information.
sections.plainLanguage: The measuring is switched off until someone turns it on. A packet cannot switch it on by itself, just as a stranger's note cannot make you start timing yourself.

sections.title: A Sample Packet Flow
sections.content:
Appendix C walks through a simple exchange. Host A sends packet 1 with PSNTP 25. Host B receives it, later sends packet 2 with PSNTP 12 and PSNLR 25, and puts the time it held the first packet in DELTATLR. The hosts do not share a clock: the RFC sets Host B an hour ahead of Host A to make this point, and only deltas travel in packets.

Host A then computes the total time from sending packet 1 to receiving packet 2 and subtracts DELTATLR. In the RFC's example, 12 minus 4 gives a round-trip delay of 8. The RFC also shows that PSNs reveal lost retransmissions: a resent TCP segment keeps the same TCP sequence number but gets a new PSN, so a gap shows packets that never arrived.
sections.plainLanguage: If I took 12 seconds to hear back and you say you waited 4 seconds before answering, the trip itself took 8 seconds.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC admits PDM may introduce new weaknesses.

  • Resource use: hosts keep per-5-tuple control blocks, so a memory limit SHOULD be implemented. PDM state lives only at end hosts, not routers or middleboxes.
  • Pervasive monitoring: PDM travels in the clear. The authors think it is of little help for reading payload content, but separating wire time from processing time might let an attacker guess an application type.
  • Covert channel: PDM fields could leak data, but the RFC sees no reason an attacker would choose it over other places. A PDM-aware middlebox or host that sees nonsensical numbers could block, discard or alert.
  • Timing attacks: PDM could help timing attacks on cryptographic protocols. Implementations should limit PDM to certain addresses or ports and SHOULD require an explicit restart of monitoring after a period (the example given is 1 hour). A user "Consent to be Measured" SHOULD be a prerequisite.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the timing notes are visible to anyone watching, they could give away clues. So the measuring should be limited, time-boxed and agreed to.

fields.name: Option Length
fields.desc: Octets after the type and length fields. MUST be 10.

fields.name: ScaleDTLR
fields.desc: Scaling value for Delta Time Last Received.

fields.name: ScaleDTLS
fields.desc: Scaling value for Delta Time Last Sent.

fields.name: PSN This Packet
fields.desc: Random start, incremented per packet of the 5-tuple flow.

fields.name: PSN Last Received
fields.desc: PSNTP of the packet last received on the 5-tuple.

fields.name: Delta Time Last Received
fields.desc: Send time of packet n minus receive time of packet n-1.

fields.name: Delta Time Last Sent
fields.desc: Receive time of packet n minus send time of packet n-1.
